title: HPV Vaccine Before Pregnancy Linked to Lower Preterm Birth Risk
excerpt: A Swedish study of 624,713 births, published in The BMJ, found mothers vaccinated against HPV before pregnancy had lower odds of preterm birth and other complications — an observational finding that stops short of proof.
body:
• A nationwide Swedish study of 624,713 first-time singleton births found mothers who received the HPV vaccine before pregnancy had statistically significant lower odds of preterm birth and other pregnancy complications.
  • The effect was modest — about 5% lower odds of preterm birth and 15% lower odds of very preterm birth (28–31 weeks) — and strongest among women vaccinated before the age of 17.
  • The study is observational, so it cannot prove vaccination caused the better outcomes; stillbirth rates were lower in vaccinated mothers but did not reach statistical significance.
  • For parents, the finding adds one more expert-backed reason to favour HPV vaccination in early adolescence, on top of its established protection against cervical cancer.

The news

Women who received the HPV vaccine before becoming pregnant had lower rates of preterm birth and several other pregnancy complications, according to a large Swedish study published in The BMJ. The population-based, matched case–control study covered 624,713 singleton births to first-time mothers aged 16 to 35 between 2006 and 2023; 92,620 of the mothers — 14.8% — had received the quadrivalent HPV vaccine (Gardasil) before pregnancy.

After adjusting for confounders, vaccination was associated with lower odds of preterm birth (adjusted odds ratio 0.95), very preterm birth between 28 and 31 weeks (0.85), spontaneous preterm birth (0.95), preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (0.93), and delivering a severely small-for-gestational-age infant (0.92). Each adverse pregnancy case was matched with up to ten controls of the same age and conception year, accounting for smoking, body mass index, education, income, maternal diagnoses, and country of birth.

Context & background

The result lands two decades after Gardasil and Cervarix were introduced amid fierce controversy. Because HPV is primarily sexually transmitted, opponents argued that vaccinating adolescents would encourage promiscuity, and unsupported claims circulated that the vaccine could harm fertility. Neither claim held up: the vaccines have dramatically cut cervical cancer in vaccinated populations, and no fertility harm emerged. This study effectively turns the old fertility claim on its head.

There was a scientific reason to look. Evidence has been building that HPV infection itself — and the procedures used to treat the cervical lesions it causes — can raise the risk of preterm birth. Several earlier studies raised the possibility that vaccination might be protective, but none was large enough to be convincing. Sweden's national health registers, tracking every birth over 18 years, finally provided the scale.

"Together with previous research showing the safety of human papillomavirus vaccination during pregnancy, our results suggest that human papillomavirus vaccination is not only safe with respect to pregnancy outcomes but may also confer additional benefits by reducing the risk of adverse events."

— Study authors, The BMJ

Impact & analysis

The headline numbers deserve careful reading. A 5% relative reduction in preterm birth is modest at the individual level, but preterm birth is common — and at population scale, small shifts prevent real suffering. The 15% reduction in very preterm birth matters more, since births before 32 weeks carry the heaviest health risks. The age gradient is the most telling detail: women vaccinated before 17 saw the largest benefit, consistent with vaccination working best when it prevents infection before first exposure — the same pattern seen in cervical cancer prevention.

The caveats are real and the authors state them plainly. This is an observational study, not a randomised trial, so it cannot prove cause and effect; vaccinated mothers may differ from unvaccinated mothers in unmeasured ways. The researchers acknowledge incomplete data on spontaneous abortions and limited investigation of the biological pathways. Stillbirth was lower but missed statistical significance.

Diaspora angle

The finding speaks directly to conversations happening in Indian households everywhere. Cervical cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer death among women in India, and adolescent HPV vaccination is the single most effective prevention — yet uptake debates often stall on safety anxieties carried over from the vaccine's early controversy. For parents weighing whether a 12- or 13-year-old needs the shot, this study adds a second, unexpected layer to the benefit side of the ledger: not only cancer protection years later, but potentially healthier pregnancies much further down the line. The age gradient reinforces what doctors already advise — vaccinate early, before exposure.

What's next

The authors call for research into the biological pathways linking HPV, cervical treatment, and preterm birth. On their reading, the evidence now supports the continued rollout of HPV vaccination in routine immunisation programmes worldwide. For readers, nothing in this study changes individual medical advice — that remains a conversation with a doctor — but it strengthens the case that was already there.
